title: When Gautamiputra Struck the Coins
subtitle: How Silver Bore the Fall of the Kshaharatas
era: Kshaharata-Satavahana conflict, date debated c. 1st-early 2nd century CE
region: Nashik, Jogalthambi and the western Deccan
moral: The evidence of defeat may be hammered into the very metal of power.

sources.citation: Jogalthambi hoard of overstruck Nahapana coins, catalogued in E. J. Rapson, British Museum coin catalogue, 1908
sources.note: Primary numismatic evidence for Gautamiputra Satakarni overstriking Nahapana's coinage.

sources.citation: Nasik Cave inscription of Gautami Balashri praising Gautamiputra Satakarni, in D. C. Sircar, Select Inscriptions, vol. 1, 1965
sources.note: Satavahana inscription claiming the Kshaharata line was rooted out.

sources.citation: R. C. C. Fynes, The Kshatrapas and the Satavahanas, Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society 5.1, 1995, pp. 39-56
sources.note: Modern discussion of the contested synchronism and chronology.

panels.shot: dramatic close-up of a silver coin on an anvil, a hammer frozen mid-strike as a new legend descends on an old king's face

dialogue.text: In the western Deccan, Nahapana’s face once shone on silver; then Gautamiputra Satakarni struck his mark upon it, and the fall of a Saka house was hammered into coin.

panels.shot: slow push-in on an open palm holding multiple bright silver coins, each bearing Nahapana’s bust and legends in Brahmi and Kharoshthi

dialogue.text: Before the overstrikes, there was only Nahapana: Kshaharata ruler, Saka satrap, his name and titles running clean on silver across the western Deccan.

panels.shot: wide aerial of the western Deccan with stylised trade routes, caravans and ships moving toward a gleaming city

dialogue.text: His coins moved with caravans and ships, from Nashik’s caves to the ports of the Konkan; silver tied Saka satraps to merchants, guilds and land.

panels.shot: medium shot inside a rock-cut cave, low-angle on Nahapana, with donors and monks around him

dialogue.text: In inscriptions near Nashik, the Kshaharata name stands firm; their satrap granted caves and land, their authority cut into stone as surely as into coin.

panels.shot: tight shot on Nahapana at a table of ledgers and coins, expression wary, shadow falling across his face

dialogue.text: But beyond his reach, Satavahana power stirred again; an old rival house, pushed back and divided, began to press once more from the eastern Deccan.

panels.shot: silhouetted long shot of two armies facing each other across a dusty plain, banners of different symbols fluttering

dialogue.text: The records do not name each battlefield, nor the exact year, but they remember a clash: Saka Kshaharatas against resurgent Satavahanas, contesting land, roads and the right to strike silver.

panels.shot: medium shot of Nahapana on horseback in armour, looking back over his shoulder toward his men

dialogue.speaker: nahapana_and_gautamiputra_satakarni
dialogue.text: Hold the roads, and the hills will follow.

panels.shot: abrupt cut to a quiet aftermath, wide shot of an abandoned satrapal camp with trampled standards and scattered coins

dialogue.text: The details of the defeat are lost, but the outcome is not: Kshaharata power broke, its lands and mints slipping into Satavahana hands.

panels.shot: interior low-angle shot of a Satavahana mint, with workers, anvils and dies; focus on one worker placing a Nahapana coin on an anvil

dialogue.text: Then came the most silent battle: not on fields, but on anvils. Gautamiputra Satakarni took Nahapana’s own coins and overstruck them with his name.

panels.shot: extreme close-up of hammer hitting the die, sparks and motion frozen, fragments of the old legend still visible beneath the new

dialogue.text: Blow by blow, old legends were flattened; new letters, ‘Gautamiputra Satakarni’, pressed themselves over faint, stubborn traces of ‘Nahapana’.

panels.shot: tabletop macro shot of several overstruck coins, one flipped to reveal ghostly under-type

dialogue.text: Today, in the Jogalthambi hoard, Nahapana’s face still lurks under those overstrikes; a rare sight where two claims to power share the same thin disk of silver.

panels.shot: medium shot in a Satavahana court, Gautamiputra’s mother seated as an inscription is being carved on a tablet

dialogue.text: In the Nasik caves, Gautami Balashri’s inscription praised her son and declared that Gautamiputra had ‘uprooted the Kshaharatas’, claiming the satrapal house was finished.

panels.shot: close-up of the stone inscription letters, hand and chisel in frame

dialogue.text: The stone speaks with the victor’s voice; it does not doubt, it does not qualify. It simply states that the Kshaharata lineage was rooted out.

panels.shot: documentary-style montage shot: scholars in a library, a hand turning a coin under a magnifying glass, another tracing an inscription rubbing

dialogue.text: Centuries later, scholars match stone to silver; the inscription’s bold claim and the overstruck Jogalthambi coins together tell how a satrap’s fall was preserved in metal.

panels.shot: thoughtful medium shot of a scholar gesturing at a timeline with uncertain ranges highlighted

dialogue.text: Yet even now, the precise date of Nahapana’s defeat is debated; the coins and caves fix the sequence, but the exact year remains a gap between them.

panels.shot: poised split-panel style shot: one side shows Nahapana regal, other shows a faint overstruck coin where he is barely visible

dialogue.text: For Nahapana, the end of his line is not written in a single battle report; it is traced in ghosts of his portrait, shrinking beneath the sharper lines of another king’s name.

panels.shot: final contemplative close-up of a human hand holding an overstruck coin against the sky, light catching both layers

dialogue.text: In that thin disk we see how power can be erased yet still endure as a shadow; the very coins once used to rule became the archive of a dynasty’s defeat.
